## Abstract

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-papillomaviruses are near-ubiquitous skin commensals, yet whether they are transcriptionally active in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is unsettled. We reanalyzed `r comma(stats$n_screened)` public human RNA sequencing libraries, typing human papillomavirus (HPV), scoring productive infection from late (L1) capsid transcripts, and controlling for cell-line origin, depth, and chemistry. Productive infection was common in warts (`r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of libraries above a viral load threshold calibrated on them) and epidermodysplasia verruciformis. cSCC and actinic keratosis libraries, although sequenced almost `r nword(stats$neo_medreads / stats$ctrl_medreads)` times more deeply, exceeded it in only `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`%, with a median viral load more than `r nword(floor(log10(stats$ctrl_medrpm / stats$neo_medrpm)))` orders of magnitude lower, and did not differ. A minority of lesions carried genuine productive beta- or alpha-HPV infection. The transcribed types were largely disjoint from the skin DNA reservoir: of its `r rv("n_dna_present")` types, `r rv("n_dna_present_silent")` were productive in no RNA library. HPV signal instead concentrated in nonprimary material: cell-line and engineered libraries had `r nword(mean(c(stats$cl_or, stats$eng_or)))`-fold higher odds of positivity (*P* < 10⁻⁷), mostly integrated HPV16 and HPV18, whereas HPV was detected in 2–3% of primary skin libraries. Cutaneous HPV is therefore productive in warts but present only at trace, transcriptionally inactive levels in healthy skin and carcinoma, which models of beta-HPV in skin cancer must explain.
